column7: description

'Ali ibn al-'Abbas al-Majusi, also known as Masoudi, or Latinized as Haly Abbas, was a Persian physician and psychologist from the Islamic Golden Age, most famous for the Kitab al-Maliki or Complete Book of the Medical Art, his textbook on medicine and psychology.
Mikyö Dorje was the eighth Karmapa, head of the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism.
Albert Venn Dicey, was a British Whig jurist and constitutional theorist.
Abbo or Abbon of Fleury, also known as Saint Abbo or Abbon, was a monk and abbot of Fleury Abbey in present-day Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire near Orléans, France.
Abhinavagupta was a philosopher, mystic and aesthetician from Kashmir.
Abner of Burgos was a Jewish philosopher, a convert to Christianity, and a polemical writer against his former religion.
Abraham Cohen de Herrera, also known as Alonso Nunez de Herrera or Abraham Irira, was a religious philosopher and cabbalist.
Abraham Maimonides was a Jewish philosopher and leader of Egyptian Jewry, and the son of Maimonides.
Abraham Tucker was an English country gentleman, who devoted himself to the study of philosophy.

Abraham bar Ḥiyya ha-Nasi, also known as Abraham Savasorda, Abraham Albargeloni, and Abraham Judaeus, was a Catalan Jewish mathematician, astronomer, philosopher, and translator who lived in Barcelona, then part of the County of Barcelona in what is now Spain.
Abraham ibn Daud was a Spanish-Jewish astronomer, historian and philosopher born in Córdoba, Spain about 1110 who was said to have been killed for his religious beliefs in Toledo, Spain about 1180.
Abraham ben Meir Ibn Ezra was one of the most distinguished Jewish biblical commentators and philosophers of the Middle Ages.
Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, also known as Rhazes, 864 or 865 – 925 or 935 CE, was a Persian physician, philosopher and alchemist who lived during the Islamic Golden Age.
Abu Hanifa was a Muslim scholar, jurist, theologian, and ascetic, and the founder and eponym of the Hanafi school of Sunni jurisprudence.

column2: Abu Hatim Ahmad ibn Hamdan al-Razi
column7: Abū Ḥātim Aḥmad ibn Ḥamdān al-Rāzī was a Persian Ismaili philosopher of the 10th century, who died in 322 AH.
Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī, full name ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbās al-Baghdadi, was an Arab intellectual, writer, and philosopher of the 10th century.
Abu Ma‘shar al-Balkhi, Latinized as Albumasar, was an early Persian Muslim astrologer, thought to be the greatest astrologer of the Abbasid court in Baghdad.
Imam Abu Mansur al-Maturidi was a Hanafi jurist and theologian who is the eponym of the Maturidi school of kalam in Sunnism.
Abu Sulayman Muhammad al-Sijistani, nicknamed al-Mantiqi, c.
Ḥabīb ibn Aws al-Ṭā’ī, better known by his sobriquet Abū Tammām, was an Arab Muslim poet.
Abu Ya'qub Ishaq ibn Ahmad al-Sijistani or al-Sijzi, also known as Bandaneh, was a 10th-century Persian Ismaili missionary active in the northern and eastern Iranian lands.
Abu Zayd Ahmed ibn Sahl Balkhi was a Persian Muslim polymath: a geographer, mathematician, physician, psychologist and scientist.
Abu al-Hakam al-Kirmani was a prominent philosopher and scholar from al-Andalus.
Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari was an Arab Muslim theologian known for being the eponymous founder of the Ash'ari school of kalam in Sunnism.
Abu al-Hassan Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Amiri was a Muslim theologian and philosopher who attempted to reconcile philosophy with religion, and Sufism with conventional Islam.
Adam Ferguson, also known as Ferguson of Raith, was a Scottish philosopher and historian of the Scottish Enlightenment.
Adam Smith was a Scottish economist and philosopher who was a pioneer in the field of political economy and key figure during the Scottish Enlightenment.
Adam of Balsham was an Anglo-Norman scholastic and churchman.
Adam of Wodeham, OFM was a philosopher and theologian.
Addison Webster Moore was a U.S. pragmatist philosopher.
Adelard of Bath was a 12th-century English natural philosopher.
Adi Shankara, also called Adi Shankaracharya, was an Indian Vedic scholar-monk, philosopher, and teacher of Advaita Vedanta.
Adolf Bernhard Philipp Reinach was a German philosopher associated with the Munich phenomenology school.
Aedesius was a Neoplatonic philosopher and mystic.
Aenesidemus was a 1st-century BC Greek Pyrrhonist philosopher from Knossos who revived the doctrines of Pyrrho and introduced ten skeptical "modes" for the suspension of judgment.
Afrikan Alexandrovich Spir, also spelled African Spir, was a Russian-born philosopher of German-Greek descent who wrote primarily in German, but also French.
Agostino Nifo was an Italian philosopher and commentator.
Agrippa was a Pyrrhonist philosopher who probably lived towards the end of the 1st century CE.
Asher Zvi Hirsch Ginsberg, primarily known by his Hebrew name and pen name Ahad Ha'am, was a Hebrew journalist and essayist, and one of the foremost pre-state Zionist thinkers.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal was an Arab jurist and founder of the Hanbali school who is widely recognized as the scholar who memorized the most Hadiths in Islamic history.
Ahmad ibn al-Tayyib al-Sarakhsi was a Persian traveler, historian and philosopher from the city of Sarakhs.
Ajita Kesakambali was an ancient Indian philosopher in the 6th century BC.
Akka Mahadevi was a 12th century philosopher, poet, mystic and a prominent member of the Lingayatism denomination of Hinduism founded in the 12th century.
Shree Akshobhya Tirtha was a Dvaita philosopher, scholar and theologian.
Jamāl ad-Dīn al-Ḥasan ibn Yūsuf ibn ʿAli ibn al-Muṭahhar al-Ḥillī, commonly known as al-Allāmah al-Ḥillī, was a Twelver Shi'a Muslim scholar and theologian of Iraqi Arab descent.
Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ṭayyib al-Bāqillānī, was a Sunni Muslim scholar and polymath who specialized in speculative Islamic theology, jurisprudence, logic, and hadith.
Abu Nasr Muhammad al-Farabi, known in the Latin West as Alpharabius, was an early Islamic philosopher and music theorist.

column6: epistemologists, ethicists, social and political philosophers
column7: Al-Ghazali, (Persian: ابو حامد محمد ابن محمد غزالی توسی, romanized: Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Ghazālī Ṭūsi, Latinized as Algazelus, was a Shafi'i Sunni Muslim Persian scholar and polymath.
Dhia' ul-Dīn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Yūsuf al-Juwaynī al-Shafi'ī was an Iranian Sunni scholar famous for being the foremost leading jurisconsult, legal theoretician and Islamic theologian of his time.
Abū Yūsuf Yaʻqūb ibn ʼIsḥāq aṣ-Ṣabbāḥ al-Kindī was a Mesopotamian Arab polymath who was active as a philosopher, mathematician, physician, and music theorist.
Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri, also known by his Latin name Abulola Moarrensis, was an Arab philosopher, poet, and writer from Ma'arrat al-Nu'man, Emirate of Aleppo.

Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Habib, commonly known by the nisba al-Mawardi, was a Sunni polymath and a Shafi'i jurist, legal theoretician, muhaddith, theologian, sociologist and an expert in political science.

Abu al-Hasan ʿAbd al-Jabbar ibn Ahmad ibn Khalil ibn ʿAbdallah al-Hamadani al-Asadabadi was a Persian Mu'tazili theologian, jurist and hadith scholar who is remembered as the Qadi al-Qudat of the Buyid dynasty, and a reported follower of the Shafi‘i school.

'Abd al-Karīm ibn Hawazin Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī al-Naysābūrī was an Arab Muslim scholar, theologian, jurist, legal theoretician, commentator of the Qur’an, muhaddith, grammarian, spiritual master, orator, poet, and an eminent scholar who mastered a number of Islamic sciences.

Al-Shafi'i (Arabic: الشَّافِعِيّ, romanized: al-Shāfiʿī; IPA: [a ʃaːfiʕiː] ;767–820 CE) was a Muslim scholar, jurist, muhaddith, traditionist, theologian, ascetic, and eponym of the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islamic jurisprudence.
Émile-Auguste Chartier, commonly known as Alain, was a French philosopher, journalist, essayist, pacifist, and teacher of philosophy.
Alain LeRoy Locke was an American writer, philosopher, and educator.
Alain de Lille was a French theologian and poet.
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the theory of relativity.
Ludwig Philipp Albert Schweitzer was a German polymath from Alsace.
Albert of Saxony was a German late medieval philosopher, mathematician, and Latin bishop known for his contributions to logic and physics.
Albertus Magnus, also known as Saint Albert the Great, Albert of Swabia, Albert von Bollstadt, or Albert of Cologne, was a German Dominican friar, philosopher, scientist, and bishop.
Albinus was a Platonist philosopher, who lived at Smyrna, and was teacher of Galen.
Alcibiades was an Athenian statesman and general.
Alcinous was a Middle Platonist philosopher.
Alcmaeon of Croton was an early Greek medical writer and philosopher-scientist.
Alcuin of York, also called Ealhwine, Alhwin, or Alchoin, was an Anglo-Saxon scholar, clergyman, poet, and teacher from York, Northumbria, who was active in the Carolingian Empire in the 8th century.
Alejandro Korn was an Argentine psychiatrist, philosopher, reformist and politician.
Aleksei Fyodorovich Losev was a Soviet and Russian philosopher, philologist and culturologist, one of the most prominent figures in Russian philosophical and religious thought of the 20th century.
Aleksey Stepanovich Khomyakov was a Russian theologian, philosopher, poet and amateur artist.
Alessandro Achillini (Latin Alexander Achillinus; 20 or 29 October 1463 – 2 August 1512) was an Italian philosopher and physician.

Alexander Bain was a Scottish philosopher and educationalist in the British school of empiricism and a prominent and innovative figure in the fields of psychology, linguistics, logic, moral philosophy and education reform.
Alexander Aleksandrovich Bogdanov, born Alexander Malinovsky, was a Russian and later Soviet physician, philosopher, science fiction writer, and Bolshevik revolutionary.
Alexander Bryan Johnson, was a British-born American philosopher and semanticist.
Alexander Gerard FRSE was a Scottish minister, academic and philosophical writer.
Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten was a German philosopher.
Alexander Ivanovich Herzen was a Russian writer and thinker known as the precursor of Russian socialism and one of the main precursors of agrarian populism.
Alexander Neckam was an English poet, theologian, and writer.
Alexander of Aphrodisias was a Peripatetic philosopher and the most celebrated of the Ancient Greek commentators on the writings of Aristotle.

Alexander of Hales—known also as Doctor Irrefragibilis, or "Irrefutable Teacher", and as Theologorum Monarcha—was a Franciscan friar, theologian, and philosopher instrumental to the development of scholasticism.

Alexandre Koyré (; French: [kwaʁe]; born Alexandr Vladimirovich Koyra; 29 August 1892 – 28 April 1964), also anglicized as Alexander Koyre, was a French philosopher of Russian origin who wrote on the history and philosophy of science.
Alexis Charles Henri Clérel, comte de Tocqueville, was a French diplomat, political philosopher and historian.
Alexius Meinong von Handschuchsheim was an Austrian philosopher, a realist known for his unique ontology and theory of objects.
Alf Niels Christian Ross was a Danish jurist, legal philosopher and judge of the European Court of Human Rights.
Albin Alfred Baeumler, was an Austrian-born German philosopher, pedagogue and prominent Nazi ideologue.

Alfred Jarry was a French symbolist writer who is best known for his play Ubu Roi, often cited as a forerunner of the Dada, Surrealist, and Futurist movements of the 1920s and 1930s and later the theatre of the absurd in the 1950s and 1960s.
Alfred Firmin Loisy was a French Catholic priest, theologian, and academic, generally regarded as one of the leading figures of the modernist movement within the Catholic Church.
Alfred North Whitehead was an English mathematician and philosopher.
Alfred Russel Wallace was an English naturalist, explorer, geographer, anthropologist and illustrator.
Alfred Schutz was an Austrian philosopher and social phenomenologist whose work bridged sociological and phenomenological traditions.
Algernon Sidney or Sydney was an English politician, republican political theorist and colonel.
Ambrose of Milan, canonized as Saint Ambrose, was a Roman theologian and statesman who served as Bishop of Milan from 374 to 397.
Ammonius Hermiae was a Greek philosopher from Alexandria, Byzantine Egypt.
Ammonius Saccas was a Hellenistic Neoplatonic self-taught philosopher from Alexandria, Roman Egypt, generally regarded as the precursor of Neoplatonism or one of its founders.
Anacharsis was a Scythian prince and philosopher of uncertain historicity who lived in the 6th century BC.
Ananda Kentish Muthu Coomaraswamy was a Ceylonese metaphysician, historian and a philosopher of Indian art who was an early interpreter of Indian culture to the West.
Ānandavardhana was a Kashmiri court poet and literary critic, honored with the title of Rajanak during King Avantivarman's reign.
Anaxagoras was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.
Anaxarchus was a Greek philosopher of the school of Democritus.
Anaxilaus or Anaxilas of Larissa was a physician and Pythagorean philosopher.
Anaximander was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who lived in Miletus, a city of Ionia.
Anaximenes of Miletus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Miletus in Anatolia.
Anders Theodor Samuel Nygren was a Swedish Lutheran theologian.
Andrea Cesalpino was a Florentine physician, philosopher and botanist.
Andronikos of Rhodes was a Greek philosopher from Rhodes who was also the scholarch of the Peripatetic school.
Anna Maria van Schurman was a Dutch painter, engraver, poet, classical scholar, philosopher, and feminist writer who is best known for her exceptional learning and her defence of female education.
Anne Conway was an English philosopher of the seventeenth century, whose work was in the tradition of the Cambridge Platonists.

Anniceris was a Cyrenaic philosopher. He argued that pleasure is achieved through individual acts of gratification which are sought for the pleasure that they produce, but he also laid great emphasis on the love of family, country, friendship and gratitude, which provide pleasure even when they dema

Anselm of Canterbury, also known as Anselm of Aosta after his birthplace and Anselm of Bec after his monastery, was a Benedictine abbot, philosopher and theologian who served as Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109.
Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury was an English Whig politician, philosopher and writer.
Anthony Collins was an English philosopher and essayist, notable for being one of the early proponents of Deism in Great Britain.
Antiochus of Ascalon was a 1st-century BC Platonist philosopher.
Antiphon of Rhamnus was the earliest of the ten Attic orators, and an important figure in fifth-century Athenian political and intellectual life.
Antisthenes was a Greek philosopher and a pupil of Socrates.
Antoine Arnauld was a French Catholic theologian, priest, philosopher and mathematician.
Antoine Augustin Cournot was a French philosopher and mathematician who contributed to the development of economics.
Antoine Le Grand was a French Recollect and Cartesian philosopher.
Anton Wilhelm Amo was a Nzema philosopher from Axim, Dutch Gold Coast then within what was broadly considered the region of Guinea.
Antonio Francesco Gramsci was an Italian Marxist philosopher, journalist and politician.
Antonio Labriola was an Italian Marxist theoretician and philosopher.
Antonio Francesco Davide Ambrogio Rosmini-Serbati, IC was an Italian Catholic priest and philosopher.

Apollonius of Tyana was a Greek philosopher and religious leader from the town of Tyana, Cappadocia in Roman Anatolia, who spent his life travelling and teaching in the Middle East, North Africa and India.
Apuleius, also called Lucius Apuleius Madaurensis, was a Numidian Latin-language prose writer, Platonist philosopher and rhetorician.
Arcesilaus was a Greek Hellenistic philosopher.
Archibald Alison was a Scottish Anglican priest and essayist.
Archimedes of Syracuse was an Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor from the city of Syracuse in Sicily.
Archytas was an Ancient Greek mathematician, music theorist, statesman, and strategist from the ancient city of Taras in modern Apulia, Southern Italy.
Aristides the Athenian was a 2nd-century Christian Greek author who is primarily known as the author of the Apology of Aristides.
Aristippus of Cyrene was a hedonistic Greek philosopher and the founder of the Cyrenaic school of philosophy.
Aristo of Chios, also spelled Ariston, was a Greek Stoic philosopher and colleague of Zeno of Citium.

column6: aestheticians, epistemologists, ethicists, logicians, metaphysicians, social and political philosophers
column7: Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath.
Aristoxenus of Tarentum was a Greek Peripatetic philosopher, and a pupil of Aristotle.
Arius was a Cyrenaic presbyter and ascetic.
Arnold Geulincx, also known by his pseudonym Philaretus, was a Flemish philosopher, metaphysician, and logician.
Arnold Ruge was a German philosopher and political writer.
Arthur Collier was an English Anglican priest and philosopher who wrote about the non-existence of an absolute external world.
Sir Arthur Stanley Eddington was an English astrophysicist and mathematician.

Arthur Oncken Lovejoy was an American philosopher and intellectual historian, who founded the discipline known as the history of ideas with his book The Great Chain of Being, on the topic of that name, which has been described as 'probably the single most influential work in the history of ideas in
Arthur Schopenhauer, also known as the “Philosopher of Pessimism”, was a German philosopher and writer.

Arthur de Gobineau, Count de Gobineau was a French writer and diplomat who is best known for helping introduce scientific race theory and "racial demography", and for developing the theory of the Aryan master race and Nordicism.
Asaṅga was one of the most important spiritual figures of Mahayana Buddhism and the founder of the Yogachara school.

Asclepiades, sometimes called Asclepiades of Bithynia or Asclepiades of Prusa, was a Greek physician born at Prusias-on-Sea in Bithynia in Anatolia and who flourished at Rome, where he practised and taught Greek medicine.
Ashtavakra is a revered Vedic sage in Hinduism.
Aspasius was a Peripatetic philosopher. Boethius, who frequently referred to his works, said he wrote commentaries on most of the works of Aristotle.

Athanasius I of Alexandria, also called Athanasius the Great, Athanasius the Confessor, or, among Coptic Christians, Athanasius the Apostolic, was a Christian theologian and the 20th Patriarch of Alexandria.
Atiśa Dīpaṃkara Śrījñāna was a Buddhist religious teacher and leader from Bengal.
Count August Dołęga Cieszkowski was a Polish philosopher, economist and social and political activist.
August Wilhelm Rehberg was a German philosopher.
Isidore Auguste Marie François Xavier Comte (; French: [oɡyst kɔ̃t] ; 19 January 1798 – 5 September 1857) was a French philosopher and writer who formulated the doctrine of positivism.
Augustine of Hippo, also well-known as Saint Augustine, was a Christian theologian and philosopher from Thagaste, Numidia Cirtensis and the Bishop of Hippo Regius.
Augustus De Morgan was a British mathematician and logician.

Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Yaḥya ibn aṣ-Ṣā’igh at-Tūjībī ibn Bājja, known simply as Ibn Bajja or his Latinized name Avempace, was an Arab polymath, whose writings include works regarding astronomy, physics, and music, as well as philosophy, medicine, botany, and poetry.

Ibn Rushd, Latinized as Averroes, was an Andalusian polymath and jurist who was proficient in a variety of intellectual fields, including philosophy, theology, medicine, astronomy, physics, psychology, mathematics, neurology, Islamic jurisprudence, law, and linguistics.
Ibn Sina, commonly known in the West as Avicenna ( AV-ih-SEN-ə), was a preeminent philosopher and physician of the Muslim world.
Axel Anders Theodor Hägerström was a Swedish philosopher.

Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was an Indian jurist, economist, social reformer and politician who chaired the committee that drafted the Constitution of India based on the debates of the Constituent Assembly of India and the first draft of Sir Benegal Narsing Rau.
Bahyā ibn Pāqudā, c. 1050–1120, was a Jewish philosopher and rabbi who lived in the Taifa of Zaragoza in al-Andalus.
Baltasar Gracián y Morales, better known as Baltasar Gracián, was a Spanish Jesuit priest and Baroque prose writer and philosopher.
Paul Thiry, Baron d'Holbach, known as d'Holbach, was a Franco-German philosopher, encyclopedist and writer, who was a prominent figure in the French Enlightenment.
Bartholomäus Keckermann (c. 1572 – 25 August 1609) was a German writer, Calvinist theologian and philosopher.
Bartolomé de Medina, was a Spanish theologian born in Medina de Rioseco, Spain.
Bartolus de Saxoferrato was an Italian law professor and one of the most prominent continental jurists of Medieval Roman Law.
Baruch Spinoza, also known under his Latinized pen name Benedictus de Spinoza, was a philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish origin who was born and lived in the Dutch Republic.

Basava, also called Basavēśvara and Basavaṇṇa, was an Indian philosopher, poet, Lingayat social reformer in the Shiva-focused bhakti movement, and a Hindu Shaivite social reformer during the reign of the Kalyani Chalukya and the Kalachuri Dynasty.

Basilides was an early Christian Gnostic religious teacher in Alexandria, Egypt who, according to Clement of Alexandria, was active between 117–161 AD, and claimed to have inherited his teachings from the apostle Saint Matthias.
Bede, OSB, also known as the Venerable Bede or Bede the Venerable, was an English Benedictine monk, author and scholar.
Benedetto Croce, was an Italian idealist philosopher, historian, and politician who wrote on numerous topics, including philosophy, history, historiography, and aesthetics.
Henri-Benjamin Constant de Rebecque, or simply Benjamin Constant, was a Swiss and French political thinker, activist and writer on political theory and religion.
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath who was one of the Founding Fathers of the United States; a drafter and signer of the Declaration of Independence; and the first postmaster general.
Benjamin Paul Blood was an American philosopher, mystic and poet.
Benjamin Peirce was an American mathematician who taught at Harvard University for approximately 50 years.
Benjamin Ricketson Tucker was an American individualist anarchist and self-identified socialist.
Benjamin Whichcote was an English Establishment and Puritan priest, Provost of King's College, Cambridge and leader of the Cambridge Platonists.
Bernard Bolzano was a Bohemian mathematician, logician, philosopher, theologian and Catholic priest of Italian extraction, also known for his liberal views.
Bernard Bosanquet was an English philosopher and political theorist, and an influential figure on matters of political and social policy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Bernard Le Bovier de Fontenelle, also called Bernard Le Bouyer de Fontenelle, was a French writer and a member of three of the academies of the Institut de France, noted especially for his accessible treatment of scientific topics during the unfolding of the Age of Enlightenment.
Bernard Mandeville, or Bernard de Mandeville, was an Anglo-Dutch philosopher, political economist, satirist, writer and physician.
Bernard of Chartres was a twelfth-century French Neo-Platonist philosopher, scholar, and administrator.

Bernard of Clairvaux, O.Cist., venerated as Saint Bernard, was an abbot, mystic, co-founder of the Knights Templar, and a major leader in the reform of the Benedictines through the nascent Cistercian Order.
Bernardino Telesio was an Italian philosopher and natural scientist.
Bernardus Silvestris, also known as Bernard Silvestris and Bernard Silvester, was a medieval Platonist philosopher and poet of the 12th century.
Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann was a German mathematician who made profound contributions to analysis, number theory, and differential geometry.

column6: epistemologists, ethicists, logicians, metaphysicians, social and political philosophers
column7: Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl Russell, was an English philosopher, logician, and social reformer.
Bessarion was a Byzantine Greek Renaissance humanist, theologian, Catholic cardinal and one of the famed Greek scholars who contributed to the revival of letters in the 15th century.
Bhartṛhari, was an Indian philosopher of language, linguist and poet, known for his contributions to the fields of linguistics, grammar, and philosophy.
Bhoja was the Paramara king of Malwa region in central India.
Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
Biagio Pelacani da Parma; c. 1350 – 1416), known in English as Blasius of Parma, was an Italian philosopher, mathematician and astrologer.
Bodhidharma was a semi-legendary Buddhist monk who lived during the 5th or 6th century CE.
Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, commonly known simply as Boethius, was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages.
Boetius de Dacia was a 13th-century Danish philosopher of the Dominican Order.
Bonaventure was an Italian Catholic Franciscan bishop, cardinal, scholastic theologian and philosopher.
Borden Parker Bowne was an American Christian philosopher, Methodist minister and theologian.
Percy Brand Blanshard was an American philosopher known primarily for his defense of rationalism and idealism.
Branislav Petronijević was a Serbian philosopher and paleontologist, and a professor at the University of Belgrade.
Bruno Bauer was a German philosopher, theologian, and historian.
Buddhaghosa was a 5th-century Indian Theravādin Buddhist commentator, translator, and philosopher.
Burchard of Worms was the bishop of the Imperial City of Worms, in the Holy Roman Empire.
Béla Hamvas was a Hungarian writer, philosopher, and social critic.
Charlie Dunbar Broad was an English philosopher who worked on epistemology, history of philosophy, philosophy of science, and ethics, as well as the philosophical aspects of psychical research.
Cyril Edwin Mitchinson Joad was an English philosopher, author, teacher and broadcasting personality.
Clarence Irving Lewis was an American academic philosopher.
Clive Staples Lewis was a British author, literary scholar and Anglican lay theologian.
Cai Yuanpei, spelt Ts'ai Yuan-p'ei during his lifetime, was a Chinese philosopher and politician who was an influential figure in the history of Chinese modern education.
Calcidius was a 4th-century philosopher who translated the first part of Plato's Timaeus from Greek into Latin around the year 321 and provided with it an extensive commentary.
Callicles is thought to have been an ancient Athenian political philosopher.
Candidus was the name given to the Anglo-Saxon Wizo or Witto by Alcuin, whose scholar he was and with whom he went in 782 to Gaul.
Carl Gustav Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist, psychotherapist, and psychologist who founded the school of analytical psychology.
Carl Linnaeus, also known after ennoblement in 1761 as Carl von Linné, was a Swedish biologist and physician who formalised binomial nomenclature, the modern system of naming organisms.
Carl Schmitt was a German jurist and political philosopher.
Carl Stumpf was a German philosopher, psychologist and musicologist.
Carlo Cattaneo was an Italian philosopher, writer, and activist, famous for his role in the Five Days of Milan in March 1848, when he led the city council during the rebellion.
Carlo Raimondo Michelstaedter or Michelstädter was an Italian philosopher, artist, and man of letters.
Carneades was a Greek philosopher, perhaps the most prominent head of the Skeptical Academy in Ancient Greece.
Cassius Longinus was a Greek rhetorician and philosophical critic.
Catharine Trotter Cockburn was an English novelist, dramatist and philosopher who wrote on various subjects, including moral philosophy and theology, and maintained a prolific correspondence.
Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti was a Florentine philosopher and father of Guido Cavalcanti, a close friend of Dante Alighieri.
Cebes of Thebes was an Ancient Greek philosopher from Thebes remembered as a disciple of Socrates.
Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity.
Cesare Beccaria Bonesana, Marquis of Gualdrasco and Villareggio was an Italian criminologist, jurist, philosopher, economist, and politician.
Cesare Cremonini, sometimes Cesare Cremonino, was an Italian academic and professor of natural philosophy.
Ch'ien Mu or Qian Mu was a Chinese historian, philosopher and writer.
Chaerephon, of the Athenian deme Sphettus, was an ancient Greek best remembered as a loyal friend and follower of Socrates.
Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, born Vishvambhara Mishra, was an Indian Hindu saint from Bengal and the founder of Gaudiya Vaishnavism.
Chakradhara (also known as Sarvajña Shri Chakradhar Swāmī or Kunwar Haripāladeva) was an Indian Hindu saint and philosopher, who was the founder of Mahanubhava sect of Krishnaism.

Chanakya, according to legendary narratives preserved in various traditions dating from the 4th to 11th century CE, was a Brahmin who assisted the first Mauryan emperor Chandragupta in his rise to power and the establishment of the Maurya Empire.
Chandrakirti or "Chandra" was a Buddhist scholar of the Madhyamaka school who was based out of the monastery of Nalanda.
Chao Cuo was a Chinese philosopher, politician, and writer.
Chapman Cohen was an English freethinker, atheist, and secularist writer and lecturer.
Charles Babbage was an English polymath. A mathematician, philosopher, inventor and mechanical engineer, Babbage originated the concept of a digital programmable computer.
Sir Charles Bell was a Scottish surgeon, anatomist, physiologist, neurologist, artist, and philosophical theologian.
Charles Bonnet was a Genevan naturalist and philosophical writer.
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, widely known for his contributions to evolutionary biology.
François Marie Charles Fourier was a French philosopher, an influential early socialist thinker, and one of the founders of utopian socialism.
Charles Hartshorne was an American philosopher who concentrated primarily on the philosophy of religion and metaphysics, but also contributed to ornithology.

Gustav Radbruch was a German legal scholar and politician.
Gustav Gustavovich Shpet was a Russian philosopher, historian of philosophy, psychologist, art theoretician, and interpreter of German and Polish descent.
Gustav Teichmüller was a German philosopher.
Gustave Belot was a French philosopher and educational administrator.
György Lukács was a Hungarian Marxist philosopher, literary historian, literary critic, and aesthetician.
Géraud de Cordemoy was a French philosopher, historian and lawyer.
Gargi Vachaknavi (Sans: गार्गी वाचक्नवी; Gārgī Vācaknavī) was an ancient Indian sage and philosopher.
Harold Arthur Prichard was an English philosopher.
Henry Habberley Price was a Welsh philosopher, known for his work on the philosophy of perception.
Helmut Richard Niebuhr was an American theologian and Protestant minister who is considered one of the most important Christian ethicists in 20th-century America.
Hadi Sabzavari or Hajj Molla Hadi Sabzavari was an Iranian Shia cleric, philosopher, mystic theologian and poet.
Hajime Tanabe was a Japanese philosopher of science, particularly of mathematics and physics.
Hamid al-Din Abu'l-Hasan Ahmad ibn Abdallah al-Kirmani was an Isma'ili scholar.
Han Fei, also known as Han Feizi or Han Fei Tzu, was a Chinese Legalist philosopher and statesman during the Warring States period.

Han Yu, courtesy name Tuizhi, and commonly known by his posthumous name Han Wengong, was an essayist, Confucian scholar, poet, and government official during the Tang dynasty who significantly influenced the development of Neo-Confucianism.
Johannes Wilhelm Cornelius was a German neo-Kantian philosopher and psychologist.
Hans Adolf Eduard Driesch was a German biologist and philosopher from Bad Kreuznach.
Johannes "Hans" Freyer was a German sociologist and philosopher of the conservative revolutionary movement.
Hans Kelsen was an Austrian and later American jurist, legal philosopher and political philosopher.
Hans Reichenbach was a leading philosopher of science, educator, and proponent of logical empiricism.

Hans Vaihinger was a German philosopher, best known as a Kant scholar and for his Die Philosophie des Als Ob, published in 1911 although its statement of basic principles had been written more than thirty years earlier.
Harald Høffding was a Danish philosopher and theologian.
Harriet Martineau was an English social theorist.
Harriet Taylor Mill was an English writer, philosopher, and women's rights advocate.
Hasdai ben Abraham Crescas was a Spanish-Jewish philosopher and a renowned halakhist.
Hastings Rashdall was an English philosopher, theologian, historian, and Anglican priest.
He Yan, courtesy name Pingshu, was a Chinese philosopher and politician of the state of Cao Wei in the Three Kingdoms period of China.
Hecato or Hecaton of Rhodes was a Greek Stoic philosopher.
Hegesias of Cyrene was a Cyrenaic philosopher.
Heinrich Christoph Wilhelm von Sigwart was a German philosopher and logician.
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim was a German Renaissance polymath, physician, legal scholar, alchemist, soldier, knight, theologian, and occult writer.
Heinrich Adam Friedrich Czolbe (30 December 1819, Katzke bei Danzig - 19 February 1873, Königsberg) was a medical doctor and materialist philosopher from the Kingdom of Prussia.
Heinrich Rudolf Hertz was a German physicist who first conclusively proved the existence of the electromagnetic waves proposed by James Clerk Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism.

Heinrich Moritz Chalybäus was a German philosopher best known for his exegetical work on philosophy, such as his characterisation of Hegel's dialectic as a triad of "thesis–antithesis–synthesis." Biography Chalybäus was born in Pfaffroda in Saxony.
Heinrich John Rickert was a German philosopher, a leading neo-Kantian of the Baden school.
Bernd Heinrich Wilhelm von Kleist was a German poet, dramatist, novelist, short story writer and journalist.
Heiric of Auxerre was a French Benedictine theologian and writer.
Hemachandra was a 11-12th century Śvetāmbara Jaina ācārya, scholar, poet, mathematician, philosopher, yogi, grammarian, law theorist, historian, lexicographer, rhetorician, logician, and prosodist.
Henri Frédéric Amiel was a Swiss moral philosopher, poet, and critic.

Henri-Louis Bergson was a French philosopher who was influential in the traditions of analytic philosophy and continental philosophy, especially during the first half of the 20th century until the Second World War, but also after 1966 when Gilles Deleuze published Le Bergsonisme.
Jules Henri Poincaré was a French mathematician, theoretical physicist, engineer, and philosopher of science.

Claude Henri de Rouvroy, Comte de Saint-Simon, better known as Henri de Saint-Simon, was a French political, economic and socialist theorist and businessman whose thought had a substantial influence on politics, economics, sociology and the philosophy of science.
Henricus Regius was a Dutch philosopher, physician, and professor of medicine at the University of Utrecht from 1638.
Henry Brewster Stanton was an American abolitionist, social reformer, attorney, journalist and politician.

column2: Henry Brougham, 1st Baron Brougham and Vaux
column7: Henry Peter Brougham, 1st Baron Brougham and Vaux, was a British statesman who became Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain and played a prominent role in passing the Reform Act 1832 and Slavery Abolition Act 1833.
Henry David Thoreau was an American naturalist, essayist, poet, and philosopher.
Henry George was an American political economist, social philosopher and journalist.
Henry Home, Lord Kames was a Scottish writer, philosopher and judge who played a major role in Scotland's Agricultural Revolution.
Henry James Sr. was an American theologian and the father of the philosopher William James, the novelist Henry James, and the diarist Alice James.
Henry Longueville Mansel was an English philosopher and ecclesiastic.
Henry More was an English philosopher, Anglican priest, theologian, and poet, associated with the Cambridge Platonists.
Henry Sidgwick was an English utilitarian philosopher and economist and is best known in philosophy for his utilitarian treatise The Methods of Ethics.
Henry Suso, OP was a German Dominican friar and the most popular vernacular writer of the fourteenth century.
Henry of Ghent, also known as Henricus de Gandavo and Henricus Gandavensis, was a scholastic philosopher who acquired the nickname of Doctor Solemnis.
Henry Harclay was an English medieval philosopher and university chancellor.
Heraclides Ponticus was a Greek philosopher and astronomer who was born in Heraclea Pontica, now Karadeniz Ereğli, Turkey, and migrated to Athens.
Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from the city of Ephesus, which was then part of the Persian Empire.
Herbert Marcuse was a German and American philosopher, social critic, and political theorist, associated with the Frankfurt School of critical theory.
Herbert Spencer was an English polymath active as a philosopher, psychologist, biologist, sociologist, and anthropologist.
Herman Dooyeweerd, also spelled Herman Dooijeweerd, was a professor of law and jurisprudence at the Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam from 1926 to 1965.

Herman of Carinthia, also called Hermannus Dalmata, Hermannus Secundus, Herman Dalmatin, or Sclavus Dalmata, by his own words born in the "heart of Istria", was a philosopher, astronomer, astrologer, mathematician and translator of Arabic works into Latin.
Hermann Bruno Otto Blumenau was a German pharmacist who founded the city of Blumenau, situated in the Itajaí-Açu river valley in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil.

Hermann Cohen was a German Jewish philosopher, one of the founders of the Marburg school of neo-Kantianism, and he is often held to be "probably the most important Jewish philosopher of the nineteenth century".
Hermann Friedrich Wilhelm Hinrichs was a German right Hegelian philosopher.
Rudolf Hermann Lotze was a German philosopher and logician.

Hermann Ulrici was a German philosopher. He was co-editor of the philosophical journal Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik.
Hermann Klaus Hugo Weyl was a German mathematician, theoretical physicist, logician and philosopher.
Hermann Ludwig Ferdinand von Helmholtz was a German physicist and physician who made significant contributions in several scientific fields, particularly hydrodynamic stability.
Hermann Alexander Graf von Keyserling was a Baltic German philosopher from the Keyserlingk family.
Hervaeus Natalis, also known as de Nédellec, was a Dominican theologian, the 14th Master of the Dominicans, and the author of a number of works on philosophy and theology.
Hicetas was a Greek philosopher of the Pythagorean School.
Hierocles was a Stoic philosopher. Very little is known about his life.

Hildegard of Bingen, also known as the "Sibyl of the Rhine", was a German Benedictine abbess and polymath, active during the High Middle Ages as a writer, composer, philosopher, mystic, visionary, and as a medical writer and practitioner of the Catholic Church.
Hillel ben Samuel was an Italian physician, philosopher, and Talmudist.
Himerius was a Greek sophist and rhetorician.
Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, was a Frankish jurist and theologian, as well as the friend, advisor and propagandist of Charles the Bald.
Hipparchia of Maroneia was a Cynic philosopher, and wife of Crates of Thebes.
Hippasus of Metapontum was a Greek philosopher and early follower of Pythagoras.
Hippias of Elis was a Greek sophist, and a contemporary of Socrates.

Hippocrates of Kos, also known as Hippocrates II, named after his grandfather Hippocrates I was a Greek physician and philosopher of the classical period who is considered one of the most outstanding figures in the history of medicine.
Hippolyte Adolphe Taine was a French historian, critic and philosopher.
Hryhorii Skovoroda, also Gregory Skovoroda or Grigory Skovoroda, was a philosopher of Ukrainian Cossack origin who lived and worked in the Russian Empire.
Hu Shih was a Chinese academic, writer, diplomat, and politician.
Huang Zongxi, courtesy name Taichong, was a Chinese naturalist, political theorist, philosopher, and soldier during the latter part of the Ming dynasty into the early part of the Qing.
Hugh Binning was a Scottish philosopher and theologian.
Hugh Blair FRSE was a Scottish minister of religion, author and rhetorician, considered one of the first great theorists of written discourse.
Hugh of Saint Victor was a German canon regular and a leading theologian and writer on mystical theology.
Hugo Albert Emil Hermann Dingler was a German scientist and philosopher.
Hugo Grotius, also known as Hugo de Groot or Huig de Groot, was a Dutch humanist, diplomat, lawyer, theologian, jurist, statesman, poet and playwright.
Hugo Stumberg Kołłątaj, also spelled Kołłątay, was a prominent Polish constitutional reformer and educationalist, and one of the most prominent figures of the Polish Enlightenment.
Hui Shi, or Huizi, was a Warring States period Chinese philosopher, and, according to the Lushi Chunqiu, a prime minister of the Wei state said to have written a code of laws.
Humphry Ditton was an English mathematician.
Hunayn ibn Ishaq al-Ibadi was an influential Iraqi Arab Church of the East Christian translator, scholar, physician, and scientist.

Hyacinthe Sigismond Gerdil, CRSP was an Italian theologian, bishop and cardinal, who was a significant figure in the response of the papacy to the assault on the Catholic Church by the upheavals caused by the French Revolution.
Hypatia was a Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer, and mathematician who lived in Alexandria, at that time in the province of Egypt and a major city of the Roman Empire.
Hyujeong, also called Seosan Daesa was a Korean Seon master.
Ivor Armstrong Richards CH, known as I. A.
Iamblichus was a Syrian Arab Neoplatonic philosopher who determined a direction later taken by Neoplatonism.
Ibn 'Arabī was a Sunni Muslim Arab scholar, Sufi mystic, poet, and Muslim philosopher from al-Andalus, who exercised notable influence within Sufi metaphysics and Islamic thought in general.
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Fūrāk, Abū Bakr al-Asbahānī al-Shāfi`ī, commonly known as Ibn Fūrāk; c.
Ibn Ḥazm was an Andalusi Muslim polymath, historian, traditionist, jurist, philosopher, and theologian, born in the Córdoban Caliphate, present-day Spain.
Sa'd ibn Mansur Ibn Kammuna (Arabic: إبن كمونة سعد إبن منصور, 1215—1284, was a 13th-century Jewish physician and philosopher.
Ibn Khaldūn was an Arab scholar, historian, philosopher, and sociologist.
Abu'l-Barakāt Hibat Allah ibn Malkā al-Baghdādī was an Islamic philosopher, physician and physicist of Jewish descent from Baghdad, Iraq.
Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Masarra ibn Najih al-Jabali was an Andalusian Muslim ascetic and scholar.
Ibn Sab'in was an Arab Sufi, philosopher from al-Andalus in the west land of Islamic world.
Ibn Taymiyya was a Sunni Muslim scholar, jurist, Mujtahid, traditionist, Qadiri Sufi, proto-Salafist theologian and iconoclast.
Ibn Ṭufayl was an Arab Andalusian Muslim polymath: a writer, physician, philosopher, theologian, astronomer, and vizier.
Ibn al-Haytham, Latinized as Alhazen, was a mathematician, astronomer, and physicist of the Islamic Golden Age from Iraq.
Abū al-Khayr al-Ḥasan ibn Suwār ibn Bābā ibn Bahnām, called Ibn al-Khammār, was an East Syriac Christian philosopher and physician who taught and worked in Baghdad.
Abū Muhammad ʿAbd Allāh Rūzbih ibn Dādūya, born Rōzbih pūr-i Dādōē, more commonly known as Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, was a Persian translator, philosopher, author and thinker who wrote in the Arabic language.
Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Ishaq al-Rawandi, commonly known as Ibn al-Rawandi, was a scholar and theologian.
Abū al-Faraj ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ṭayyib, known by the nisba al-ʿIrāqī and in medieval Latin as Abulpharagius Abdalla Benattibus, was a prolific writer, priest and polymath of the Church of the East.
Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār ibn Hāni‘ an-Naẓẓām was an Arab Mu'tazilite theologian and poet.
Immanuel Hermann Fichte was a German philosopher and son of Johann Gottlieb Fichte.

column6: aestheticians, epistemologists, ethicists, metaphysicians, social and political philosophers
column7: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher. Born in Königsberg in the Kingdom of Prussia, he is considered one of the central thinkers of the Enlightenment.
Immanuel ben Solomon ben Jekuthiel of Rome was a Jewish poet and writer who lived in the Papal States and composed works in Hebrew and Italian.
Ioane Petritsi, also referred as John Petritzos, was a Georgian Neoplatonic philosopher of the 11th–12th century.
Isaac ben Judah Abarbanel, commonly referred to as Abarbanel, was a Portuguese Jewish statesman, philosopher, Bible commentator, and financier.
Isaac Cardoso was a Portuguese-born Sephardic Jewish physician, philosopher and polemic writer based in Verona.
Isaac Israeli ben Solomon, also known as Isaac Israeli the Elder and Isaac Judaeus, was a Jewish physician and philosopher.
Isaac La Peyrère, also known as Isaac de La Peyrère or Pererius, was a French-born theologian, writer, and lawyer.
Sir Isaac Newton was an English polymath who was a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, alchemist, theologian, author and inventor.
Balthazar Orobio de Castro, was a Portuguese Jewish philosopher, physician and religious apologist.
Isaac ben Joseph ibn Pulgar or Isaac ben Joseph ibn Polkar or Isaac Polqar was a Spanish Jewish philosopher, poet, and controversialist, who flourished in the first half of the fourteenth century.
Isaac ben Moses Arama was a Spanish rabbi and author.

Isaac de Pinto was a Dutch merchant and banker of Portuguese Sephardic Jewish origin who was one of the main investors in the Dutch East India Company, as well as a scholar and philosophe who concentrated on Jewish emancipation and national debt.
Isidore of Seville was a Hispano-Roman scholar, theologian and archbishop of Seville.
Isocrates was an ancient Greek rhetorician, one of the ten Attic orators.
Yisrael ben Ze'ev Wolf Lipkin, also known as Israel Salanter or Yisroel Salanter, was the father of the Musar movement in Orthodox Judaism and a famed Rosh yeshiva and Talmudist.
Itō Jinsai (伊藤 仁斎; Japanese pronunciation: [i.toːʑiꜜɰ̃.sai], August 30, 1627, Kyoto, Japan – April 5, 1705, Kyoto), who also went by the pen name Keisai, was a Japanese Confucian philosopher.
Ivan Alexandrovich Ilyin was a Russian jurist, religious and political philosopher, publicist, orator, and a far-right thinker.
John Henry Muirhead was a Scottish philosopher best known for having initiated the Muirhead Library of Philosophy in 1890.
John McTaggart Ellis McTaggart was an English philosopher most known for his work in idealism, philosophy of time, and metaphysics.
Abū Mūsā Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, died c. 806−816, is the purported author of a large number of works in Arabic, often called the Jabirian corpus.
Carl Jacob Christoph Burckhardt was a Swiss historian of art and culture and an influential figure in the historiography of both fields.
Jacob Friedrich von Abel was a German philosopher.
Jacobus Arminius was a Dutch Reformed minister and theologian during the Protestant Reformation period whose views became the basis of Arminianism and the Dutch Remonstrant movement.
Jacopo Mazzoni was an Italian philosopher, a professor in Pisa, and friend of Galileo Galilei.
Giacomo Zabarella was an Italian Aristotelian philosopher and logician.
Jacques Maritain was a French Catholic philosopher and theologian.
Jacques Rohault was a French philosopher, physicist and mathematician, and a follower of Cartesianism.
Jahm bin Safwan was an Islamic theologian of the Umayyad period and whose name has given rise to the Jahmiyya moniker.
Jaimini was an ancient Indian scholar who founded the Mīmāṃsā school of Hindu philosophy.
Jakob Böhme was a German philosopher, Christian mystic, and Lutheran Protestant theologian.
Jakob Friedrich Fries was a German post-Kantian philosopher and mathematician.
Jakob Lorber was a Christian mystic and self-professed visionary from the Duchy of Styria who promoted liberal Universalism, and who referred to himself as "God's scribe".
Jakob Sigismund Beck was a German philosopher.
Jalal al-Din al-Dawani, also known as Allama Davani, was a theologian, philosopher, jurist, and poet, who is considered to have been one of the leading scholars in late 15th-century Iran.

Sayyid Jamāl al-Dīn al-Afghānī, also known as Jamāl ad-Dīn Asadābādī and commonly known as Al-Afghani, was a political activist and Islamic ideologist who travelled throughout the Muslim world during the late 19th century.
James Beattie was a Scottish poet, moralist, and philosopher.
James Bryce, 1st Viscount Bryce,, was a British academic, jurist, historian, diplomat, and Liberal politician.
James Burnett, Lord Monboddo was a Scottish judge, scholar of linguistic evolution, philosopher and deist.

James Clerk Maxwell was a Scottish physicist and mathematician who was responsible for the classical theory of electromagnetic radiation, which was the first theory to describe electricity, magnetism and light as different manifestations of the same phenomenon.
James Dalrymple, 1st Viscount Stair was a Scottish lawyer and statesman, and a key influence on the Scottish Enlightenment.
James Edwin Creighton was an American idealist philosopher, Cornell academic.
James Frederick Ferrier was a Scottish metaphysical writer and philosopher.
James Harrington was an English political theorist known for his contributions to classical republican thought.
James Hutchison Stirling was a Scottish idealist philosopher and physician.

James Mark Baldwin was an American philosopher and psychologist who was educated at Princeton under the supervision of Scottish philosopher James McCosh and who was one of the founders of the Department of Psychology at Princeton and the University of Toronto.
James Martineau was a British religious philosopher influential in the history of Unitarianism.
James McCosh was a philosopher of the Scottish School of Common Sense.
James Mill was a Scottish historian, economist, and political theorist, who was a founder of the Ricardian school of economics.
James Sully was an English psychologist, philosopher and writer.
James Ward was an English psychologist and philosopher.
James of Viterbo, born Giacomo Capocci, was an Italian Roman Catholic Augustinian friar and Scholastic theologian, who later became Archbishop of Naples.

Jan Hus, sometimes anglicized as John Goose or John Huss, and referred to in historical texts as Iohannes Hus or Johannes Huss, was a Czech Christian theologian and philosopher who became a Church reformer and the inspiration of Hussitism, a key predecessor to Protestantism, and a seminal figure in
Jan Leopold Łukasiewicz was a Polish logician, and philosopher who is best known for Polish notation and Łukasiewicz logic.
Jan Śniadecki was a Polish mathematician, philosopher, and astronomer at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries.
Jayanta Bhatta was a poet, teacher, logician, and an advisor to King Sankaravarman of Kashmir.
Jayatirtha, also known as Teekacharya, was a Hindu philosopher, dialectician, polemicist and the sixth pontiff of Madhvacharya Peetha from.
Tsongkhapa was an influential Tibetan Buddhist monk, philosopher, and tantric yogi, whose activities led to the formation of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism.
Jean-Baptiste Pierre Antoine de Monet, chevalier de Lamarck, often known simply as Lamarck, was a French naturalist, biologist, academic, and soldier.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a Genevan philosopher, philosophe, writer, and composer.
Jean-Pierre de Crousaz was a Swiss theologian and philosopher.

Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin was a French lawyer and politician, who, as the author of Physiologie du goût, became celebrated for his culinary reminiscences and reflections on the craft and science of cookery and the art of eating.
Jean Bodin was a French jurist and political philosopher, member of the Parlement of Paris and professor of law at the University of Toulouse.
Jean Buridan was an influential 14th‑century French scholastic philosopher.

Jean Charlier de Gerson was a French Roman Catholic scholar, educator, reformer, and poet, Chancellor of the University of Paris, a guiding influence of the conciliar movement and one of the most prominent theologians at the Council of Constance.
Jean Le Clerc, also Johannes Clericus, was a Genevan theologian, biblical scholar, and journalist.
Jean Le Rond d'Alembert was a French mathematician, physicist, philosopher, and music theorist.
Jean William Fritz Piaget was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
Jean André Wahl was a French philosopher.
Jeremy Bentham was an English philosopher, jurist, and social reformer regarded as the founder of modern utilitarianism.
Jerome New Frank was an American legal philosopher and author who played a leading role in the legal realism movement.
Jesus, also known as Jesus Christ, Jesus of Nazareth, and by various other names and titles, was a 1st-century Jewish preacher and religious leader in the Roman province of Judaea.
Ji Kang, sometimes referred to as Xi Kang, courtesy name Shuye, was a Chinese composer, essayist, philosopher, and poet of the Three Kingdoms period.

Jia Yi was a Chinese essayist, poet and politician of the Western Han dynasty, best known as one of the earliest known writers of fu rhapsody and for his essay "Disquisition Finding Fault with Qin", which criticises the Qin dynasty and describes Jia's opinions on the reasons for its collapse.
Jiddu Krishnamurti was an Indian spiritual figure, speaker, and writer.
Jinul Puril Bojo Daesa, often called Jinul or Chinul for short, was a Korean monk of the Goryeo period, who is considered to be the most influential figure in the formation of Korean Seon Buddhism.
Joachim Jungius was a German mathematician, logician and philosopher of science.
Joachim of Fiore, also known as Joachim of Flora, was an Italian Christian theologian, Catholic abbot, and the founder of the monastic order of San Giovanni in Fiore.
Johann Augustus Eberhard was a German theologian and "popular philosopher".
Johann Friedrich Herbart was a German philosopher, psychologist and founder of pedagogy as an academic discipline.
Johann Georg Hamann was a German Lutheran philosopher from Königsberg.
Johann Gottfried von Herder was a German philosopher, theologian, pastor, poet, and literary critic.
Johann Gottlieb Fichte was a German philosopher, and a founding figure of German idealism, which developed from the theoretical and ethical writings of Immanuel Kant.
Johann Heinrich Abicht was a German philosopher.

Johann Heinrich Lambert was an Alsatian polymath from the Republic of Mulhouse—then an associate of the Swiss Confederacy—who made fundamental contributions to mathematics, physics, philosophy, astronomy, and map projections.
Johann Ulrich von Cramer was an eminent German judge, legal scholar, and Enlightenment philosopher.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
Johannes Clauberg was a German philosopher and theologian.
Johannes Crellius was a Polish and German theologian.
Johannes Kepler was a German polymath who was an astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, natural philosopher and music theorist.
Johannes Nikolaus Tetens was a German-Danish philosopher, statistician and scientist.
Johannes Tauler OP was a German mystic, a Catholic priest and a theologian.
John Abercrombie was a Scottish physician, author, philosopher and philanthropist.
John Adams was a Founding Father and the second president of the United States from 1797 to 1801.
John Allen was an eighteenth and nineteenth century political and historical writer, and Master of the College of God's Gift in Dulwich.
John Amos Comenius was a Moravian philosopher, pedagogue and theologian who is considered the father of modern education.
John Anderson was a Scottish philosopher who occupied the post of Challis Professor of Philosophy at Sydney University from 1927 to 1958.
John Austin was an English legal theorist who posthumously influenced British and American law with an analytical approach to jurisprudence and a theory of legal positivism.
John Broadus Watson was an American psychologist who popularized the scientific theory of behaviorism, establishing it as a psychological school.
John Balguy was an English divine and philosopher.
John Ballantyne was a Scottish minister of religion.
John Calvin was a French theologian, pastor and reformer in Geneva during the Protestant Reformation.
John Capreolus, in French Jean Capréolus and in Latin Johannes Capreolus, was a French Dominican theologian and Thomist.
John Cook Wilson was an English philosopher, Wykeham Professor of Logic and Fellow of New College.
John Dewey was an American philosopher, psychologist, and educational reformer.
John Elof Boodin was a Swedish-born American philosopher and educator.
John Fiske was an American philosopher and historian.
John Gneisenau Neihardt was an American writer and poet, amateur historian and ethnographer.
John Gay was an English poet and dramatist and member of the Scriblerus Club.
John Grote was an English moral philosopher and Anglican clergyman.
John Henry Newman was an English Catholic theologian, academic, philosopher, historian, writer, and poet.

Sir John Frederick William Herschel, 1st Baronet was an English polymath active as a mathematician, astronomer, chemist, inventor and experimental photographer who invented the blueprint and did botanical work.
John Hoppus FRS was an English Congregational minister, author, Fellow of the Royal Society, abolitionist and educational reformer.
John Lewis was a British Unitarian minister and Marxist philosopher and author of many works on philosophy, anthropology, and religion.

column6: epistemologists, ethicists, social and political philosophers
column7: John Locke was an English philosopher and physician, widely regarded as one of the most influential of the Enlightenment thinkers and commonly known as the "father of liberalism".
John Macmurray was a Scottish philosopher.
John Major was a Scottish philosopher, theologian, and historian who was admired and influential.
John Maynard Keynes, 1st Baron Keynes, was an English economist whose writings are considered the basis for the school of thought known as Keynesian economics, as well as its various offshoots.
John Millar of Glasgow was a Scottish philosopher, historian and Regius Professor of Civil Law at the University of Glasgow from 1761 to 1800.
John Norris, sometimes called John Norris of Bemerton, was an English theologian, philosopher and poet associated with the Cambridge Platonists.
John Peckham was a Franciscan friar and Archbishop of Canterbury in the years 1279–1292.

John Philoponus, also known as John the Grammarian or John of Alexandria, was a Greek-speaking philologist, Aristotelian commentator and Christian theologian from Alexandria, Byzantine Egypt, who authored a number of philosophical treatises and theological works.
John Ray was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
John Scotus Eriugena, also known as Johannes Scotus Erigena, John the Scot or John the Irish-born, was an Irish Neoplatonist philosopher, theologian and poet of the Early Middle Ages.
John Selden was an English jurist, a scholar of England's ancient laws and constitution and scholar of Jewish law.
John Sergeant was an English Roman Catholic priest, controversialist and theologian.

column6: ethicists, logicians, social and political philosophers
column7: John Stuart Mill was an English philosopher, political economist, and politician.
John Theophilus Desaguliers was a French-born British natural philosopher, clergyman, engineer and freemason who was elected to the Royal Society in 1714 as experimental assistant to Isaac Newton.

John Toland was an Irish rationalist philosopher and freethinker, and occasional satirist, who wrote numerous books and pamphlets on political philosophy and philosophy of religion, which are early expressions of the philosophy of the Age of Enlightenment.

John Veitch, Scottish philosopher, poet and historian: John was born in Peebles; the only son of Peninsular War veteran James Veitch and his wife, Nancy Ritchie; a woman, steeped in the folk traditions of the Borders; he was educated at the University of Edinburgh.
John Venn, FRS, FSA was an English mathematician, logician and philosopher noted for introducing Venn diagrams, which are used in logic, set theory, probability, statistics, and computer science.
John Witherspoon was a Scottish-American Presbyterian minister, educator, farmer, and a Founding Father of the United States.
John Wood Oman, FBA was a Scottish theologian and Presbyterian minister.
John Wycliffe was an English scholastic philosopher, Christian reformer, Catholic priest, and a theology professor at the University of Oxford.
John of Damascus or John Damascene, born Yūḥana ibn Manṣūr ibn Sarjūn, was a Christian monk, priest, hymnographer, and apologist.
John of Jandun or John of Jaudun was a French philosopher, theologian, and political writer.
